```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(mysteryroster)
```

Every other function in this package's no-gold-standard family --
`attribute_agreement()`, `attribute_consensus_tier()`,
`attribute_lead_lag_matrix()`, and the rest -- deliberately never names a
value as "correct." That is a design rule, stated explicitly in the
README: agreement, timing, and stability are relative claims about a
comparison set, not verdicts.

`attribute_truth_fusion()` is a different kind of thing, introduced
alongside this vignette: it *does* predict a value, with an explicit
score, and the explicit option to refuse rather than guess. This is the
first phase of a larger truth-discovery extension (future phases add
probabilistic backends that learn per-source reliability); this phase
implements exactly one method, `"majority"`, entirely in R.

## The evidence schema

Every truth-fusion function expects one long-format table: one row per
`entity_id` / `attribute` / `source_id` / `reference_year` claim.
`attribute_claims_validate()` checks that shape and reports on it
without silently repairing anything:

```{r validate}
claims <- data.frame(
  entity_id = c("1", "1", "1", "2", "2"),
  attribute = "state",
  source_id = c("nppes", "dac", "dac", "nppes", "op"),
  claimed_value = c("CO", "CO", "NM", "NY", "NY"),
  reference_year = 2024
)
validated <- attribute_claims_validate(claims)
attr(validated, "report")
```

NPI 1's `dac` row appears twice with two different values (`CO` and
`NM`) -- a legitimate claim of two real locations, not an error. The
report counts it as one `duplicate_source_years` *and* one
`multi_value_source_years`, and keeps both rows rather than collapsing
them. `on_duplicate = "error"` is available when you want duplicates to
stop the call instead, but it does not distinguish the two cases --
check the report first.

## Majority vote, with abstention

`attribute_truth_fusion()` votes by *source*, not by row: a source that
submitted the same value twice only counts once, and a source with two
legitimate values votes for both rather than being forced to pick one.

```{r fusion}
fusion_result <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "majority")
fusion_result
fusion_result$predictions
fusion_result$candidate_scores
```

NPI 1 has three votes across two values (`CO` from `nppes` and `dac`,
`NM` from `dac`'s second claim) -- `CO` wins 2 of 3, so it is predicted
with `model_score = 0.6667`. NPI 2's two sources agree outright
(`model_score = 1`). A genuine tie behaves differently:

```{r fusion-tie}
tied_claims <- data.frame(
  entity_id = "3", attribute = "state",
  source_id = c("nppes", "dac"), claimed_value = c("NY", "NJ"),
  reference_year = 2024
)
suppressMessages(attribute_truth_fusion(tied_claims, method = "majority"))$predictions
```

A true 1-1 tie always abstains (`abstention_reason = "tied_vote"`) --
there is no principled winner to report, so `predicted_value` is `NA`
rather than an arbitrary pick. Setting `abstain_threshold` abstains a
*non-tied* but weak majority too:

```{r fusion-threshold}
weak_majority <- data.frame(
  entity_id = "4", attribute = "state",
  source_id = c("a", "b", "c"), claimed_value = c("CO", "CO", "NM"),
  reference_year = 2024
)
suppressMessages(
  attribute_truth_fusion(weak_majority, method = "majority", abstain_threshold = 0.8)
)$predictions[, c("predicted_value", "model_score", "abstained", "abstention_reason")]
```

Two of three sources agreeing (67%) is a real majority, but below the
80% threshold requested here, so the call abstains anyway rather than
reporting a prediction the caller asked to treat as too weak to trust.

## One source, two conflicting claims

A source can legitimately report more than one value for the same
entity-attribute-year -- two real practice locations, say. Whether that
source then votes for both, or is excluded as unresolved, is governed
by `on_source_conflict`, and the two policies give different answers on
the same data:

```{r conflict-setup}
conflicted <- data.frame(
  entity_id = c("1", "1", "1"), attribute = "state",
  source_id = c("multi", "multi", "other"),
  claimed_value = c("CO", "NM", "CO"), reference_year = 2024
)
```

```{r conflict-single}
suppressMessages(attribute_truth_fusion(conflicted, method = "majority"))$predictions[
  , c("predicted_value", "model_score", "n_sources", "n_sources_excluded")
]
```

`on_source_conflict = "single_value"` is the default: `multi`'s claim is
internally conflicted (`CO` and `NM` for the same entity-year), so it is
excluded from voting entirely -- `n_sources_excluded = 1` -- leaving
only `other`'s single vote. The prediction is `CO`, but because `other`
alone, not because `multi` broke the tie in its favor.

```{r conflict-multi}
suppressMessages(
  attribute_truth_fusion(conflicted, method = "majority", on_source_conflict = "multi_value")
)$candidate_scores
```

`on_source_conflict = "multi_value"` instead lets `multi` vote for both
values -- appropriate when more than one value can legitimately be true
at once, but note that `model_score` under this policy is a share of
*votes cast*, not a probability that one categorical value is correct,
since `multi` contributed to two different candidates' counts.

## What's implemented, and what isn't yet

`attribute_truth_backends()` is a static capability report, not a live
probe -- it never claims a method is available before it is actually
wired up:

```{r backends}
attribute_truth_backends()
```

Only `"majority"` is implemented in this version, entirely in R
(`backend = "r_native"`). Passing an unimplemented `method`, or a
`backend` that does not match what a method actually requires, is an
error -- never a silent substitution of a different algorithm than the
one requested:

```{r backend-error, error = TRUE}
attribute_truth_fusion(claims, method = "dawid_skene")
```

Later phases are expected to add probabilistic backends (`crowd-kit`'s
Dawid-Skene, `truthdiscovery`'s TruthFinder and friends) that learn
per-source reliability rather than treating every source's vote
equally -- `source_diagnostics` is already part of the returned
object's shape for exactly that purpose, and is simply empty for
`"majority"`, which learns no such thing:

```{r source-diagnostics}
fusion_result$source_diagnostics
```

## What this does and doesn't establish

A majority-vote prediction is still a claim about what *most sources
say*, not a verified fact -- three sources repeating one outdated
address can outvote one recently corrected source, and nothing here
detects that on its own (that is exactly the kind of question
`attribute_lead_lag_matrix()` and `attribute_agreement_by_spell_age()`,
in `vignette("consensus-and-corroboration")`, are built to investigate
directly). Treat `attribute_truth_fusion()`'s output as a prediction
with an explicit, inspectable score and an honest abstention path --
not as a replacement for asking why sources disagree in the first
place.
